utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: A few housekeeping issues before we start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry we couldn't hear. First of all, either yesterday or day, Mr. Milovancevic, we were talking about an application for confidential material in this case. It's a pity Mr. Whiting is not here; I think he is the one who raised the matter. And you indicated, Mr. Milovancevic, that you were hearing of that application for the first time in court, here, that day. Registry has provided proof of delivery of that application to the Defence and it was delivered to one Predrag Milovancevic. Do you know him? On the 30th of May, 2006, at 1656.14 seconds. Do you remember -- do you know that gentleman, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is me. Thank you. However, this is what my assistant, Mr. Sekulic, is in charge of and I told you then that he wasn't there at the moment and at the moment I was addressing you I did not have that information. I don't have any doubt -- any reason to doubt that this information that you have just shared with us is correct. So this is me and I'm that person. And as far as the Defence counsel is concerned, I spoke to Mr. Sekulic. We looked at the material, and we are not opposed to that request. We are in agreement with that request. Thank you, and please accept my apologies for this situation. I hope I've managed to explain how this came about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. That's fine. That will be fine -- the purpose of asking was just to make sure that we make -- we make you aware you have received the document. Thank you so much. Then we'll hear from the Prosecution, either when Mr. Whiting is present or if the other members are privy to this issue they can tell us what the Prosecution intends to do. Yes, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just to inform the Chamber that we have filed the response just a little while ago, so it's now being processed with the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The next question, again coming back to you, Mr. Milovancevic, and I ask this with trepidation; I don't usually ask this kind of question. But in the interests of expeditiousness, I'm going to have to ask you this question. Are you able to say at this stage whether the Defence will be filing a 98 bis application or not? If I'm putting you in a spot, please feel free.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will gladly answer this question, if I'm able to. As far as seeking approval of the Trial Chamber, we spoke about that. I'm talking about the certification. We have some difficulties at this moment, and I believe that we will do it by Friday. I'm sure that we will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, we're talking at cross-purposes. I'm talking about a 98 bis, you're talking about a certification. Certification is the next item I'm coming to. Can we deal with 98 bis first?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we're talking about the submission on the oral notification of the Defence counsel, if that is what you had in mind, Your Honours, this is something that we have to submit after the lapse of five months into trial. And we have been working here at full speed. We will need some time for this kind of oral submission. If I have understood your question well, we are talking about you Rule 98 bis, and the Rule 98 bis that I have before me deals with the oral decisions of the Chamber after both parties have been heard. If this is what we are talking about, although I'm not sure, I have my reservations about that, I have the text of the rule before me. This is a translation from English into B/C/S, and I'm looking at this Rule 98 bis. This has to do with acquittal. And it says here: "At the close of the Prosecutor's case, the Trial Chamber shall by oral decisions on -- after hearing the oral submissions of the parties enter a judgement." If you're asking about our arguments and if this is what we're talking about, and if you want to hear about our oral submissions, then this is what I can tell you at the moment. We will probably need some ten days or so. Your Honour, at this moment, our situation is compounded by the status of Mr. Babic's testimony and the fact that the Prosecution case is still ongoing. There will be a lot more problems with regard to the number of victims, the nature of victims. So I really don't know what the Prosecution still wants to do, what is still their case, but judging at what has been presented so far, this is very serious. We're dealing with several thousands of pages of transcript, and we would require some time to look at all that and this is the position on the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The chickens have come back home to roost. As I said at the beginning, I shouldn't have asked this question. We are obviously at cross-purposes, Mr. Milovancevic. You are now asking for ten days. Remember, we've giving a scheduling order and that scheduling order stands. It deals with the question of 98 bis. All I wanted to know was whether or not the Defence does intend making that 98 bis application. And -- that's all I wanted to find out. And I think let's leave the matter at that point because what you have said is now complicating the whole issue and I wouldn't like to go into all those things that you have mentioned. Let me then go to the third point. Yes? Did you want to say something, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a short sentence. With regard to the scheduling order, we sent a submission earlier today and I have nothing further to add to that. I have heard your instruction and I am sorry that I went beyond the scope of your question in my previous argument. This was not my intention. The rule itself --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, that's fine, Mr. Milovancevic. I understand. I'm not finding fault with you; I'm just regretting raising the issue. Your submissions on certification -- I beg your pardon -- yeah, on certification I have -- I beg your pardon, on scheduling we haven't seen. So that's why I -- I said that the scheduling order stands because we hadn't seen -- we haven't seen them. Personally I haven't seen them. On the Babic certification, you indicated the other day that the Defence is going to be noting an appeal. Just to mention to you that your last day is the 16th of this month, and that being so I wanted to find out from the Prosecution whether any response could be filed from their side, at least by the 19th? That's Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You'll do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. The last point I wanted to raise with the parties is about the testimony of Witness MM-080. I guess the parties will have been -- will have received transcripts of that witness's testimony, most of which the Chamber feels was given in private session, when in fact it could have been given in open session. The Chamber has given -- has asked that you be given those -- that transcript, so you exercise your mind on it whether you agree with the Chamber, and if you don't make your submissions. And if you -- and if you don't make those submissions, then the Chamber will have to lift the embargo on those parts that are highlighted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask that we have until tomorrow to make those submissions? Mr. Whiting is out of the country right now, and he is the one most familiar with this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would that be okay by you, Mr. Milovancevic, until tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we can do it right now and we can say that we agree with the position of the Chamber. We have only tried to honour the measures that are applied to the witness and this is what has been a bit of a problem. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. We'll hear from the Prosecution tomorrow and then we'll deal with that part. That brings me to the end housekeeping matters from the Bench. Any from your side? Nothing from your side, Mr. Milovancevic? Who do I look at, Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'll be calling the next witness, if she could be brought in, her name is Sanja Risovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sanja Risovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Ms. Risovic, can you hear me okay? Are you receiving interpretation through the headphones?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: I can hear you. I am receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's begin. Will you please state your full name for the record -- is your -- are you having a problem with the headphones?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: I have a problem. It's been on and off. The interpretation has been on and off.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you hear me -- can you hear me now okay?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: This here, this one here -- I can hear you but the reception is not so good on one side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you for mentioning that. We'll give you a new set of headphones and see if that solves the problem. Perhaps that's a little better. Can you understand me now?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is better.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And if you do have any more problems, please don't hesitate to raise it with me.

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Would you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Sanja Risovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: On what day were you born?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on 9 December 1964.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Vinkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In 1990 you went to work for the Croatian Railways in Vinkovci. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And when did you move to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: I moved to Zagreb in November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you have any children, Ms. Risovic?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: I have a daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When was she born, on what date?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: My daughter was born on 1st January 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention now to the 2nd of May, 1995. First of all, can you tell us what the day was like on the 2nd of May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: The day was a lovely spring day, a sunny day, very nice day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And where were you on that morning?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: Since I was on maternity leave, I was on my way to my GP, and then I went to my work-place, to the Croatian Railways to the department where I used to work. And then I went down-town, to the centre of town, to the centre of Zagreb, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the atmosphere there in the centre of Zagreb on the morning of May 2nd, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: There were a lot of people moving about, people going to work, children going to school. Nothing out of the ordinary. Women going to the green market. There were a lot of people in the streets. The day was really lovely, and there were lots of strollers as a result of that, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Had there been any warning or any indication that there could be an attack on Zagreb on that day?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was none. Everything was normal as far as I could see. The people that I worked with all came to work. My GP was in her office. The trams were running, as on any other day. Everything was normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What, in fact, happened that morning?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: On my way back, I found myself at Tomislav Square in front of the railway station. I was standing at a tram stop. I was waiting for my tram to go home. I was in a hurry because I had a young child at home, so I spent a very short time in town. And before I got on the tram, I heard an explosion. I saw fire, smoke. I was looking towards Zrinjevac. And we all assumed that there had been an explosion. People were surprised. Tram came. I got on and I went home. As I came home, I said to everybody there that something had exploded down-town and that we should turn on the TV to watch the noon news. And it was then that I heard that there had been an attack on Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What did you see on the news that day?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: I saw cars ablaze, people carrying wounded, bloody persons. I saw a tram that had been hit. They were showing the wounded and the streets that had been hit, and I realised that I had been quite close to the area because the distance between those sites and the place where I was standing at the tram stop was about 200 to 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Were you injured at all on the 2nd of May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't wounded on the 2nd of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just one more question before we turn our attention to the 3rd of May. On the evening of May 2nd, 1995, did you see any news reports or any media that evening?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: I did. I was watching the prime-time news report. Everybody was interested in what was going on. We were still a country at war, and we were all following the news closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And in the evening, did they continue to report about the events of that morning that you had described as seeing on the news earlier in the day? Did that coverage continue in the evening as well?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did. They were reporting on the numbers of those killed and wounded. They were reporting on the hospitals that had received the wounded, who were all civilians. The streets involved were in the centre of town. It was quite a shock. There was a lot of news coverage of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me -- thank you. Let me turn your attention now to the 3rd of May, the very next day. Did you have something planned for that day?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had plans for the day. I gave birth to my child on the 1st of January, 1995, whereupon my child was inoculated, but my child wasn't feeling well so I was given an appointment on the 3rd of May, 1995, where my child's pediatrician was going to decide whether the child was going to be vaccinated again because the vaccination was due on the fourth month of -- rather, four months after the child's birth. And I knew that I was supposed to go to the children's hospital, Klaiceva, on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If you notice me pausing, I'm just waiting for the interpretation, just so that's clear to you. So did you go to this appointment at the children's hospital on Klaiceva?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Who were --

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: The following day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just ask a question. Is Klaiceva a suburb of Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a street in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's a street in Zagreb. While I'm at it, let me just ask this other one to you. Zrinjevac, is that a suburb or a street? The witness said: "I saw fire, smoke, I was looking towards Zrinjevac, and we all assumed there had been an explosion." Z-r-i-n-j-e-v-a-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Ms. Risovic, if you heard His Honour's question, could you please just state the name of that place or that street again and tell us what it is, please.

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: The Tomislav Square is the square that is situated in front of the railway station in the centre of town. Next to the square there's the park called Zrinjevac park. The name of the street is -- the first section is called Tomislav Square and then the name changes. At any rate, it's a park and on the right-hand side of the park there's the county court. It's the centre of town, and can be found on the axis running from the Ban Jelacic Square to the central railway station in Zagreb. It's an open area with parks and trees and monuments. I don't know if I've been clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: More than enough. Thank you so much. You may continue, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Ms. Risovic, thanks for the explanation. Who went with you, if anyone, to the children's hospital on the 3rd of May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: My brother went along, my child, and myself. We were going to the doctor's by car. By brother was taking me there for the medical check-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please tell us what happened while you were at the children's hospital.

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: We arrived at the children's hospital some 15 times ahead of the scheduled meeting, which was at 10.30. We got into the waiting-room, handed the medical documentation. I found a vacant seat, I sat down, and I was waiting. This is a children's hospital and doctors tend to be late or tend to be away because they have to attend to a child, and then they tend to be away for quite a while. I sat down on the chair, whereas my child was there with me. We had a blanket and we had everything. My brother was there to help me because he was very, very concerned about my daughter. He thought she was so small, a 4-month-old child. He was even carrying her. Then the time had come for me to change her nappies, and then I fed her. Eventually she fell asleep. A bit before 12.00 the doctor arrived. She went into her office. With me in the waiting-room there was another mom with her child, who was quite upset and crying all the time. The doctor then said that she would receive that child first because my daughter was asleep. As they went into the office I was trying to arrange all the -- all my belongings that I had, all the things that I needed for my child, so that I would be ready to go in. My brother kept hurrying me in collecting these items because he was hoping that we would thus be able to speed things along. I asked him to go over to the office itself to see whether the lady who was inside was finished or not so that I could go over and come with my daughter. I apologise. At the moment he was about to move and I was lifting Anamaria, Anamaria is my daughter's name, as I lifted her in my arms, I heard a blast. I heard the window-panes getting smashed -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It's okay. Take your time. Perhaps the usher can hand you a Kleenex.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, please. Maybe if the witness maybe would like a -- a moment to compose herself and we can adjourn for five, ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Ms. Risovic, if you can hear me, if you want to take a break now, we can take a break for a few minutes or we can continue. It's entirely up to you; whatever makes you feel more comfortable.

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Forgive me, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There's nothing to apologise for. Thank you very much, Ms. Risovic. We are concerned that you be comfortable. Would you like some time to compose yourself? Shall we stop a little bit? I suggest we stop for five, ten minutes. Court adjourned. --- Break taken at 2.58 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you feel better now, Ms. Risovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. If you feel again overwhelmed by emotion, please just indicate and we will take a break. Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Before I resume the examination, on the issue of breaks, when would Your Honour like us to -- should we take the regular break at 3.30, or should we go a little beyond that since we just had a break? What's your preference, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Our preference is that maybe we take our break at the regular time so that we don't get out of sync with the normal schedule. I notice that it's only seven minutes to go, but so be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Ms. Risovic, I realise that these are painful memories for you, so I'm sorry to ask you to go back to this. But just before the break you told us how you heard a blast and you heard window-panes getting smashed. Now, can you please continue. Tell us what happened at that point.

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: As I was holding the child in my arms, I went forward. There was a table blocking my way. I pushed it aside and I maybe made one step only. At that point I felt as if someone had hit me on my back. I don't know how to explain this. As if someone had taken a chair and hit me with it. I had the child in my arms and I was bending over. I was hunched a bit. I can't really say how long this lasted. I didn't have the feeling of the time. I was standing there with my child, and next to me there was a man. I don't even recall his face. I just told him: Please, take my child. I think everybody must have been in shock because nobody reacted to what I said, and I was unable to move at all. I wasn't able to move my right leg. I retreated. I went back and there was a wall there. I leaned against the wall and slid down. I started yelling out, calling my brother. He came to me. I told him to take Anamaria and take her somewhere safe. I wanted at least the two of them to be safe. As he took the child from my arms, I noticed that my child's head was covered in blood. I was terribly shocked. Before calling my brother, she burst into tears. And as I tried to hush her, she simply went silent. I wasn't even sure whether my child was still alive or what her condition was. My brother went running away with her and then returned after a while. I kept telling him "go away, go away," because I was afraid that again there was going to be another attack and at least I wanted -- if someone had to die, I wanted it to be me. He was thinking aloud at the time, what was he going to do with me, where should he take me, where were the doctors. Then one doctor came to us. This was of course the paediatrician's office, and there was another lady doctor, she had blonde hair, and they called some other staff to help them and they took me upstairs to the children's hospital surgery ward. There they undressed me, they X-rayed the upper part of my body. I realised at that point that something was wrong with my black. They placed compresses on the wound and they placed me on stretchers and took me outside. Then I could hear them calling all the centres in Zagreb to see which of the hospitals had a team ready to come and pick us up. There were three of us in the corridor, three of us who were wounded. I know that I was the first one to be taken away. I was taken to the Vinogradska hospital in Zagreb, to the surgery ward there. I was a bit of a trouble to them because I kept asking after my daughter. I didn't know what had happened to her. I asked every single physician who approached me to give a ring to Klaiceva hospital to inquire after my daughter. They were trying to explain to me that they -- there was no time for me to dally, that all the phone lines were down, that I had to sign the papers allowing them to operate on me. I know that the one lady physician was urging me to simply place a cross on the papers because I was unable to move my right arm and I was all covered in blood. At one point then, though, they told me that my child was fine, that she was very well, that they were in a shelter, and that I should just place that cross on the papers, and that they would then take me to the surgery theatre, and that was when I went into surgery.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Ms. Risovic, I think that's a good stopping point for the time being. We have -- have to take a break, according to our ordinary procedures, and then we'll come back and I'll just have a few more questions for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think this is a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take a short break. We'll come back at 4.00, Ms. Risovic. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Black, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe before you proceed, I just wanted to suggest that maybe we can take ten minutes off the next break just to try and cover up, so if we can break at 25 past instead of quarter past. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Absolutely. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Ms. Risovic, can you hear me okay? Can you understand me clearly?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: I hear you and I understand you clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What injuries did you suffer as a result of this experience which you've just described to us on the 3rd of May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: I was wounded in the right shoulder blade so that one part of my back muscle was removed as well as my shoulder blade. My ribs were fractured, my lungs was also injured. I had a haemotosis of the lung. I had -- in the lumbar region on the right side, I had a shrapnel there which was wedged in the stomach muscle or some muscle there. I was wounded in the right leg and the left foot, on the toes of the left foot, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I -- just very quickly, I'd like to show you two photographs. The first one has the ERN 05051029.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could see that in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Ms. Risovic, are you able to see the photograph on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And does that show -- is that you, does that show the injury to your back?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my back.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could we show the next -- the next document, please. It's 05051030.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Is that another photograph of your back and shoulder area?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: It is indeed. This is a photo of my back.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And just for the record, were these two photos taken of you yesterday when you came to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These were taken yesterday when I arrived here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could these be admitted into evidence, please? I guess two separate exhibit numbers because they are two separate documents in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the two pictures please be given two separate exhibit numbers. They are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be exhibits number 794 and exhibits number 795, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Ms. Risovic, how long -- just before the last break you explained that you went into surgery. How long were you actually in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: I stayed in the hospital until the 16th of June, and then I was transferred to Krapinska Toplica for rehabilitation and I stayed there until the month of August, until the 10th of August when I was discharged. I may have been mistaken on the date of discharge from the spa, but I know that I was discharged from the hospital on the 16th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How many surgeries have you had altogether since -- since you were injured?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: Since I was injured, I have had a total of 11 surgical procedures. I had six separate surgical corrections on the back performed by plastic surgeons. When I was wounded, I had two surgeries. Then my hand had to be operated on, some fragments of metal had to be removed. All in all, I've had 11 surgical procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: At this time, do you still have any rehabilitation work or are you having any ongoing treatment to this day?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: Every year I have to spend three weeks in re habilitation and I'm also being treated for rheumatoid arthritis which is a congenital disease, but it is aggravated by stress and shock. And that is why my hands are deformed, my fists that is. I have to work on my muscles, especially on the right-hand side because I am a typical right-handed person. I work with my right hand every day, and there are still some things that I'm not able to do on my own without other people's help.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Have these injuries affected your ability to work?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: They have. Sometimes I find it very difficult to have to do a lot of writing or if I have to work hard I sometimes suffer pain in the back. I find it very difficult to remain seated. Generally speaking, I am not allowed to carry any weight in my right hand. For example, today I was in a situation to have to wash my hair, and I can only do it when one arm, one hand. I cannot lift my right hand above my head. I had to go to -- to look for a hair-dresser just to find somebody who will wash my hair. And these are problems that I encounter in my everyday life. There are a lot of things I am not able to do in my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Have the injuries had any impact on your ability to take care of your young daughter?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: Of course they have. My child was 4 months old at the time. When I decided to have the child, I wanted to be her mother, I wanted to extend all my love and tenderness to her, to be with her. And at one point I was no longer able to be with her. And when I was eventually discharged, I couldn't carry my child. I couldn't change her diapers because for a long time I could not move my right hand. I could not feed my baby. At the end of the day, my motherhood, a lot of it, a good part of my motherhood, was spent at various hospitals in rehabilitation. And at one point my child was asked at the kindergarten where her mother was. She said: My mother lives at home in a green building and in a hotel. The green building was the hospital and a hotel was the spa. I was shocked. I didn't understand how she could say something like that, but it only made sense because if the -- her mother didn't live with her, she perceived the places where I was as my home. I spent very little time with her, unfortunately, and all my life I will regret the fact that I did not spend more time with my baby. Every mother wants to spend as much time with their child as they possibly can, to nurture and to look after their baby. And in my life there came a time when I could not look after my child in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Ms. Risovic, I'm getting close to the end of my questions. I'd like to show you a couple of photographs, and with the assistance of the court officer and the usher, if we could see trial exhibit 387, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While we're seeing trial exhibit 387, Ms. Risovic, you just mentioned a little earlier that you can't sit for a long time. Is that -- did I hear you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you feel tired while you are sitting there, please do let us know so we give you time to move about and get better. Okay? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before my testimony I took some painkillers, and I will be all right, I hope. I believe that I'll be able to sit through my testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Ms. Risovic, if you can see the photographs on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could perhaps blow-up photograph F-1, please, if we could zoom in on that a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Ms. Risovic, can you recognise this place in photograph F-1?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: This is the main entrance into the children's hospital Klaiceva -- in Klaiceva Street. On the right-hand side you can see the kiosk, in the middle there is the entrance, and on the left-hand side there is the optician's store.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page of the document, please. I'm looking for photograph F-3.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the main entrance through which you entered the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And if we could go a couple of pages ahead, please, to photograph F-8.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you recognise that place, Ms. Risovic?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: This is the corridor -- actually, the waiting-room, where I was when I was at the Klaiceva hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm done with that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the waiting-room.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Ms. Risovic, have you watched any part of this trial on television?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have, a good part of it. I have followed the information about this trial. I have read things in the papers, I've watched the news, and there are regular reports on teletext, so every evening I read what is going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And have you had any reaction while watching the trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't see a point in this question, the witness's reaction to the reports on this trial. The witness is a fact witness and she is here to tell us what she experienced and what she knows about the event that took place 11 years ago. And now the Prosecutor is asking the witness about her impressions of the trial. Maybe he should ask her what she thinks about me, my co-counsel, the Trial Chamber. Is that what he's aiming for?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think it -- there's any reason to be facetious or sarcastic. I expect -- I can't say what the witness's answer will be for sure, but I think she has some evidence which would go to remorse or lack of remorse which are factors in sentencing, Your Honour, and therefore I think they're relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Our problem is -- do you have any reply to that, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My learned friend is examining his witness about the remorse of the accused, I suppose, before we have heard the Defence case. Very interesting, Your Honours, really very, very interesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may respond, that's the procedure here. There's not a separate sentencing phase, that's not the way things work here. Sentencing is wrapped up in the evidence as we go along. Our case is almost over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's -- I was just about to ask that question, and for that reason I'll allow the question to stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Ms. Risovic, if you remember the question, I was asking you if you'd had any reaction to anything in this trial that you've seen as you followed it.

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do have a reaction to this trial that I've been following. I'm very sorry for any person who dies, gets sick, or killed for -- no matter what reason. I empathise with all the emotions of all people, and at one point I was really unnerved by the fact that the accused, Mr. Milan Martic, when Mr. Milosevic killed himself, was depressed. I always wondered if he was ever depressed when many people were harmed, for example, me and many others over the course of those two days or during the whole war. And this is what I was bothered me. I was depressed when all this happened. I am experiencing a very hard time to this very day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you do understand, though, that Mr. Milosevic didn't kill himself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He died.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpretation said: You said he killed himself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence does not have any questions of this witness, Ms. Risovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ms. Risovic, I am going to ask you a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You told us that when you looked at your baby in your brother's arms you saw blood on her head. Did you get to find out whether she was injured or not? Let me put the question differently. Did you get to find out what -- where that blood had come from?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: I managed to find out where the blood had come from. That evening, after I was operated on, I woke up and I always inquired after my child, how she was, what had happened. And then my parents and my brother brought her to the hospital so I could see her through the glass partition, as I was in the ICU. They wanted me to see that she was okay, that she was only slightly injured on the middle finger of the left hand. That same evening the baby was also operated on for that injury. And then in order to put my mind at rest and to help me go through my ordeal, they brought the child over to the hospital, for me to see her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I understand you to be saying that the blood that you had seen on her head had come from the injury on the finger?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. That blood on her head was from my injury. Her head was very close to my right shoulder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What work did you used to do at the railways before the injuries?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: I was an administrative worker and I still do the same thing, but now, although I work full time, I work at a somewhat lower intensity. They have provided me with a computer, with an anatomic chair. My work conditions have been improved to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: To accommodate your health condition?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. If I may add something, Your Honour. In Croatia people with a high degree of disability, if there's still work they are allowed some adjustments that are in keeping with their health conditions. That is why at my work-place they have provided me with some facilities to accommodate my needs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know whether your brother was injured on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: I know my brother was not injured. At that moment when the shell hit, he was already behind a wall. In the waiting-room the roof is made of glass, but he was already behind a wall and he could not be injured by the shell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I remember your testimony well, I think you indicated that when you were transferred there were three of you ladies who were injured. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: No. I said that there were three persons, and later on I learned that one of them was a woman and the other person was a male. I only -- I said that there were three persons, if I'm not mistaken, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thanks for correcting me. Did you get to know who they were?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. One of them was Ms. Mirna Kostovic, who was injured before the Croatian national theatre; and Mr. Zvonko Bakula was the other person and he was in charge of maintenance in Klaiceva hospital. He was in charge of the heating system or something. He had been injured in the courtyard of that hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you get to know the extent of their injuries?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: As for Ms. Kostovic's injury, I know that she sustained serious injuries but I don't know what the nature of those was; and Mr. Bakula, I met him later on in the hospital, in Vinogradska hospital, where we were both hospitalised, and I know that he also suffered injuries to his lateral right side, that he was injured in the back, in the legs. He is older than me and he was retired. He was retired on account of his injuries, so he no longer works, he is no longer in employment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know if any other people beyond the three of you were injured in this hospital?

utterances.speaker: SANJA RISOVIC
utterances.text: I know, I know that a pregnant lady was injured in the waiting-room. In the waiting-room where I was, there's a gynaecolocical office, then a paediatric office, an ENT office, an X-ray office. I know that a pregnant lady was injured. In front of the hospital a policeman was killed. I know that some children were injured but I don't know how many of them. I know that one or two sustained injuries or lacerations from the fragmented glass. I don't know of anybody else who was injured in that hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Risovic. That concludes my questions. Mr. Black, any questions arising?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: None, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, any questions arising?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Risovic, this brings us to the end of your testimony. On behalf of the Tribunal, let me take this opportunity to thank you for coming to testify. We thank you very much for your testimony and we hope that you get better in your health. We thank you so much. You may stand down. You are excused from further attending court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Richterova will handle the next witness. May I be excused from the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are accused, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution will call Ivan Mikulcic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May Ivan Mikulcic please come through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated, sir. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Are you receiving interpretation through the earphones? Can you hear properly?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: My name is Ivan Mikulcic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of July, 1938.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulcic, I would like to turn your attention to the events in May 1995. Where did you live in May 1995, which village?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: The village of Pleso, Mikulcica Street, 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell us where this village is located, in respect to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: In the vicinity of Velika Gorica and some 500 metres from the airport as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to refer you to the page 38 of the concise atlas, and you would see the village of Pleso in the right bottom corner. And it's grid E3.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You stated that there was an airport. Is it -- are you referring to Zagreb airport?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: Precisely so, the Zagreb airport.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: At this airport, to your knowledge, were there any armed forces stationed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: I don't know of any armed forces being stationed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You don't know whether Croatian armed forces were stationed there. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: I don't know that the Croatian armed forces were stationed there. I only know that UNPROFOR was stationed there that year.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to turn your attention to the 2nd of May. Where were you in the morning of that day?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: On that day, the 2nd of May, 1995, I was at my home at Pleso, Mikulciceva Street, 17 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 17 is the number, not 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Who was there with you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: My wife, Stefica, with our granddaughter, who was 9 months old at the time, my granddaughter Lucija.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what happened that morning.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: On that morning at around 10.00, shelling started, and an unexploded cluster bomb of the Orkan type landed in my yard about 8 metres away from me and it impacted the ground entering the ground some 3 and a half metres. Some of the bomblets of the bomb remained unexploded, but there was one that exploded some 4 metres behind my back, injuring me and damaging my home.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You started saying that day shelling started and this bomb landed on your property. Where were you at the moment when the bomb landed on your property?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: At that point, I was on my to the shelter and I only managed to get hold of the door-knob when I felt this very sharp pain in my back. And to this day I've been carrying three pieces of shrapnel in my back.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Does it mean that you were outside of your house at that moment?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, outdoors, in front of the entrance to the cellar.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And where was your wife with your granddaughter at that moment?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: I told her to follow me along to the shelter because we had heard the sound of explosions, but she basically saved herself by not listening to me immediately. She stayed inside the house and she was holding our granddaughter by her hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You stated that you felt this very sharp pain in your back, you were injured. What happened after that? What did you do after you felt this pain?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: I went over to my neighbour's, then I started feeling the heat in my back and I touched my back and then I realised that I was bleeding. I went to my neighbour, Ivica Zlodi, who took me over to the emergency clinic at Velika Gorica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness a medical report. It's ERN 03562337.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, in a moment you will see on your screen a document.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see it and I understand what it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we please scroll down?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Does it describe what kind of injury you sustained?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: This is the exact description of it, and I am in possession of the original documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We also have an English translation of this document. I don't know whether the Judges have seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you please describe briefly what kind of injuries you sustained, because many parts of this document are in Latin. Can you describe where this -- the injury you sustained?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: How shall I put it now? In my back to the left of the spine and to the right of the spine, I had pieces of shrapnel, whereas one was lodged between the fourth and the fifth vertebrae which was -- and so there is two of them and none of them have been actually taken to this day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Will you explain why these shrapnels of metal were not taken out of your body.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: I, myself, put this same question to the physician. I believe his name was Romic. And then he told me that they had to X-ray me twice because they weren't sure the first time, and he told me that they were thus placed that they would cause more damage by taking them out than by leaving them there. He told me only if I started feeling uncomfortable and feeling pain, that only then would I be operated on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 796, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did this injury have any influence on your working ability?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: Yes, largely. It largely did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can I show the witness document 03562335. Can you scroll it down a little bit? A little bit more?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In the part with the explanation, it says: "The cited first decision granted the above-named petitioner the status of civilian war invalid of group X with 20 per cent permanent disability." Is it correct -- true?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: That's true. Apparently every two years I'm entitled to a review of my status, and I find it quite ridiculous that they say that it's going to be permanently established at 20 per cent because they told me that I might have difficulties, that my situation may be aggravated, even today. So my status should be open to change.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 797, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, when you were in hospital, what kind of treatment did you receive?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: I didn't receive any treatment in terms of having been hospitalised because I wasn't hospitalised, I was simply X-rayed. My wounds were dressed, and I was discharged. I might have spent some two hours there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you -- did you go back to your house after you were discharged from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: The Velika Gorica ambulance took me home.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you -- when you arrive home, what were you able to observe, the -- first around your house and then in your neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: It was only then that I fully took in what had happened. There was this Zastava car outside, the so-called Fico. All the tires were punctured, the front left door had been destroyed, then the garage door, all the window-panes were shattered. All the -- as for the car itself, so all the oil tank, the gas tank had all been punctured and destroyed. Now, as for the house itself, both doors to the cellar were destroyed, including the large window behind these doors, even the lamp in our living room had been destroyed. Since several rockets landed, the bomblets were exploding everywhere around so that the neighbouring houses were also damaged. Of course, at the time we weren't aware of what was precisely going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness a map. It is 65 ter Exhibit Number 1683. And if we could go to page 21, the ERN number should be 2444, the four last digits. Unfortunately I think this copy on e-court looks worse than the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, can you see the map in front of you? Can you please -- are you ail to indicate where your street is on this map?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: Of course I can. This is my street, Mikulciceva Street.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And can you also indicate which house on this street is yours.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: The fifth house on the right-hand side from this street down there, so this one here. The fifth house.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: There is a little star on this map. What does it indicate, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's difficult for me to say what this stands for. Perhaps bomblet or the entire rocket landed there. This should be the site at which the Orkan rocket system landed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was there more than one bomb which land in that area, in that neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: First we have to clarify one thing. This was a rocket system of the Orkan cluster bomb which normally opens up in the air, and then bomblets fall out of it over the entire area. And these bomblets were landing all around my house covering a diameter of at least 200 metres. So all the houses that were within the diameter of 200 metres were damaged by these bomblets.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And can you -- can you also please indicate which direction is the Zagreb airport?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: In this direction, here. Should I write it down?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Is it -- we can see there is a street called Aerodromska. Is it before this street or behind this street?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: Would you please repeat your question. I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The direction you indicated, you can see that there is a street called Aerodromska. Is the airport behind this street or still before this street?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: If you're looking at the area with Zagreb at your back, then it would be in front of the Aerodromska Street.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Please could you explain that also. Seeing from top down, as here, where would the airport be and where would Zagreb be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The airport is here where I marked the area, and Zagreb is over there. That's how the street goes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you -- do you mean towards the top of this map? We can --

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: Zagreb is to the west.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We can see on this map there is orientation, west, north, east --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Going to the airport from your house, would you cross that street called Aerodromska ul, or would you get to the airport before crossing that street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What can I tell you? I can reach the airport along two routes. I can, for instance, go from my street to the main street, going to the right and then to the left, and then this is how I could reach the airport on foot. If I take the car, then I could take Mikulciceva street, Plepeliceva Street, then the Aerodromska Street, and then that's how I would get to the airport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Once you're on Aerodromska Street, would the airport be to your left -- to the west or to the east of Aerodromska Street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once I am on the Aerodromska Street, then the airport is to my left, it's on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which is west? Would that be the western side? Would it be towards the side of Zagreb or on the eastern side of Aerodromska Street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's to the west, as I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to tender this document into evidence. Can we save the markings and tender this map into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The map with markings made on it, which must be saved, is admitted into evidence and may it please be given an exhibit number -- wait a minute. Before we admit it I have one question to ask. Mr. Mikulcic, on this map here I see a lot of small dots smaller than the one star that you showed us behind your house. What would those be? Do you see those little dots, smaller stars than --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. I can see three of them here. If -- you're referring to the stars?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, I see three stars, but then there are smaller dots than the stars, which are many more around the houses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know what this could be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see them and I suppose that those stand for bomblets which came out of the cluster bombs once they opened in the air and landed in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May it -- may the exhibit be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 798, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulcic, when you returned home, did you speak to your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Everyone wanted to know if my wounds were critical, but I reassured them, but of course people were concerned, people were curious as to whether I had to go for another check-up at the hospital or not, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And could you tell us, what was their reaction to what happened in their neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: The reaction was that of sadness and embitteredness. Their roofs were damaged, their households suffered, their window-panes were damaged. I was wounded. There was no reason to be joyful, so to put it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And my last question: Had there been any warning that there was going to be such an attack, such a shelling?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was no warning, and if there had been I would not be sitting here today. I would have found shelter before the attack came.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I concluded my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. I am attorney Predrag Milovancevic, representing Mr. Martic. And now we shall embark on the so-called cross-examination. Since we both speak the same language, for the interpreters can you pause before you answer my questions. I'll try to bear that in mind and I'm very grateful to you for your cooperation. In the statement given to the OTP as a witness, it says that you are retired. When were you retired, Mr. Mikulcic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: On the 31st of December, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you were born in the village called Pleso, in the vicinity of Zagreb. Does the airport bear the same name, Pleso? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: No, you are not right. The official name of the airport is the Zagreb Airport, although the locals tend to call it the Pleso airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "us locals call it Pleso," does that mean that this is a common name of the airport or is it just a local name?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: The official name of the airport is the Zagreb Airport, and we locals call it Pleso.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the OTP you also said that in 1991 during the war in Croatia you had been mobilised, that you performed certain duties in the civilian protection unit, and that you had some tasks in the village of Pleso. These tasks in the village of Pleso, do they have anything to do with the airport?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: None whatsoever. I was mobilised to the war hospital, which was part of the Velika Gorica medical centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the OTP you also explained that your house is some 500 metres from the Zagreb airport or the Pleso airport as you call it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: The Zagreb airport. And as the crow flies - and I did not measure it - according to my free estimate, it's about 5 to 600 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You've also told us that the UNPROFOR occupied the military part of the airport?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that they occupied it. They were stationed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In that sense I used the word that is in your statement, but thank you for the explanation. When you say that the UNPROFOR was stationed in the military part of the airport, does that mean that this airport, even before the UNPROFOR arrived this, also had a military function?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: I said that the UNPROFOR was stationed at the Zagreb airport at the time. Whether they were in the military part or the civilian part, I wouldn't be able to tell you, sir, because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the usher assist us with distributing Mr. Mikulcic's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulcic, before you is your statement. The first part may be in English, I'm not sure. In any case, your statement contains one part in your mother tongue and the other part is the translation into English. If the first part is in English, then go on and find the part which is in your own language. Do you have the statement that you gave to the OTP under your name?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This is the statement given on the 27th of April, 2004. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the text of the statement after the personal data that you provided, there is your statement. And in the second paragraph you say, in the second sentence: "I know the United Nations protection force took over the military part of this airport." You explained how this happened. "And in 1995 there were many UN civilians and soldiers, but you don't know whether the Croatian army or air force was based at Pleso camp at that time." With regard to that part of your statement, this is what I would like to ask you. Even before the UNPROFOR arrived, was the Pleso an airport with a military part? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that. That's what I was aware of, that there was the Croatian army there or anyone's army. There was no army there until UNPROFOR, the United Nations, arrived, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please follow my question closely. When you say that the UNPROFOR arrived in the military part of the airport, can you please tell us when was it that the UNPROFOR arrived in the military part of the airport? Do you remember the year?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to say. It's like asking me what day was it the 2nd of May when I was wounded. I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: With regard to your explanation that the UNPROFOR arrived in the military part of the airport, I'm asking you whether this was the -- I'm not asking you whether this was the Croatian military part of the airport; I'm asking you whether the Pleso airport had its military part even before 1991.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. The Zagreb airport is partly a civilian airport, and it was partly used by the military. It was used by both.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This is exactly the gist of my question. I may have not put my question clearly enough. In the third paragraph you say that on the 2nd of May when the explosion happened and when you were injured, the -- that the morning was peaceful and that as far as you know there were no military operations around Zagreb at the time. Were there military operations elsewhere at the time? Did you hear anything or saw on TV?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything and I can't tell you what I don't know. I took the solemn declaration here that I will speak the truth and nothing but the truth, so I can't tell you because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hear, for example, that on the 1st of May the Operation Flash started, a joint operation by the Croatian armed forces and the police on -- in Western Slavonia. Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I cannot deny that. I heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: With this regard I would like to know whether there were TV reports on those operations and what was going on.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: If there were, I did not watch that. I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with the military operation in Western Slavonia, did the Ministry of Defence or the Ministry of Police or the government of Croatia provide any instruction to the population of Zagreb, the civilian population of Zagreb, as to how to behave under war conditions? Before you were injured did you have any instructions as to how to behave at the beginning of May 1995?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: What you're asking me now I did not have. However, I have something else that we as the civilian protection were aware of, and that is if there was to be shelling that we should seek shelter and that we should switch off lights in our rooms to -- because there were other shellings. This was not the only shelling. For example, the seat of the government had been shelled before that, and it is a notorious fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On that day, the 2nd of May, 1995, when these explosions were heard, did you hear the alert before that, the military alert?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, nothing could be heard. There was no alert sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained, Mr. Mikulcic, that you experienced pain in the back, you saw that you were injured, you were hospitalised. And did I understand you well when you said that you were taken to the hospital, that you were seen by the doctor, and that you were returned by the ambulance home on the same day?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: You can read this on my discharge letter, you just have to read it. It tells you exactly when I came to the outpatient hospital in Velika Gorica, when I was taken to the Rebro hospital in Zagreb, and when I was discharged and returned home. You can read it clear in my discharge letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Since it reads that in your discharge letter --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see Exhibit 796 on the screen. We had it a little while ago. This is the discharge letter from the clinical hospital centre Rebro, Zagreb. The date is 2nd of May 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the upper right-hand corner, and it is not very legible, does it say --

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does say the time of arrival -- first of all, the date of arrival at the hospital 1100 hours, the time of discharge, 1300 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: Not at all, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we look at the following document and it is 03562338 in B/C/S. So that is one document behind this, by the number sequence. This document that is now before you says that on the 4th of May, the 5th of May, 1995, the 8th of May, the 9th of May, the 10th of May, the 11th, 12th, 15, and 19 of May, I don't know whether I was too fast?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: No, you were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That on that days you went to the hospital to see the physician for check-ups. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: Can I please correct you? I didn't go anywhere. I was taken by car. I was in such condition that I had to be transported either by ambulance or my son-in-law took me, that is my daughter's husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Under the 4th of May, 1995, it says that your wounds were dressed on that day, it says evacuation; treatment, Klavocin, three times one a day; Florin three times one a day; and check-up on the 5th of May at 1000 hours. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The next date is 5th of May, 1995. Again, like on any other date that I have just quoted to you, it says that your wounds were dressed, that you received some recommendations, that you recommended to stay in bed. Is that what it says in these reports?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: Yes, it says "check-up, dressing," again another check-up on the 10th of May, dressing. I can't read this too well, so I can't be of anymore assistance in that respect. And now it says here that I need to go -- undergo check-ups, that my wounds need to be tended to, dressed. I can now see it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We just saw a document in which it says that your disability degree is 20 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we again see the same document on the screen. The number is 03562335, two pages before the last one and the title of the document is "decision."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the middle part decision. Can we scroll up a little to see the explanation.
