It transpires from this that you were granted the status of a civilian war invalid of group X with 20 per cent permanent disability, giving you the right to a set disability benefit. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with this decision on disability, I would like to ask you whether you personally know how the doctors qualified your injury, the injury that you had sustained. Is that a light -- slight injury, a severe injury? Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: I was taken where I was taken, and then I went to the medical board in Zagreb, I don't know where exactly, and there were a few doctors there making up a team. They looked at me, they checked my condition, they said it is 20 per cent. What could I do? What could I say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because there is a police report, a report of the police of the town of Zagreb, in which the wounds that certain persons had sustained are listed. And in your case it says that you sustained slight bodily harm. Do you know anything of that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything of that but let me just tell you this. If this is a slight injury, you can look at my X-ray and see that I have a shrapnel between the lumbar 4 and lumbar 5 vertebra. And if you say this is a slight injury, then be it so, but the doctors did not want to remove it because they said that it would be more harm than benefit. It's still there, the shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulcic, I'm just checking what was written in the report of the OTP material that was discussed with another witness. And we looked at the complete report on the activities that took place on the 2nd and the 3rd of May, and on page 23 of this report it says that this was in the area of the Pleso airport, that there were no persons with serious injuries, and that there was just one case of a slight injury, Mikulcic, Ivan, who was born on 18 July, and your personal datas are listed, and it says that you were extended medical help at the clinical centre of Rebro in Zagreb. Your date of birth is in this report listed as 18 July 1957.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: No, that's not when I was born. My name is Ivan Mikulcic. I was born on the 18th of July, 1938.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. All of this happened on the 2nd of May, 1995. After having been treated you returned home, and there you found the damages which you explained. Was there any other thing happening in -- at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was, on the 3rd of May, in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was the alarm sounded at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On the 2nd of May did the military or civilian authorities issue any instructions to the population in terms of cautioning them about the possible attacks?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: The citizens were warned that if there was going to be another attack, that they take additional care to go into shelters, but of course one couldn't predict that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have completed my cross-examination. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There won't be any re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Richterova. Judge? Mr. Mikulcic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mikulcic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I tried to say that. If I failed, please bear with me. I try very hard to pronounce names correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Mikulcic --

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, no problem there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You -- when you were being asked questions by the Prosecutor, you lamented the fact that the doctors are not changing your position and yet they keep saying you must come once every year for a check-up and you feel that your position is going to change, it can't stay at 20 per cent disability. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I remember that, absolutely. But if I may correct something. I found it out only the other day that I was entitled to a review of my status every two years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that, Mr. -- What I want to say, if it's any comfort to you, I just wanted to say to you that maybe every time -- while they ask you to come for a check-up is to check whether your status has changed or not and to adjust your disability percentage accordingly. Don't you think that could be the reason now that you are not on treatment any longer?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: I believe you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Am I right to say you're not on treatment any longer?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not. I'm -- the only thing that there is that I'm taking are the painkillers, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any other homes damaged in your area on this day that you may have observed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: Of course there were. I said so in my statement, and I can tell you precisely who these were: Zvonko Celindic, my neighbour; my neighbour, Anto Zgrbic; my neighbour, Stjepan and Ibica Zlodi; my neighbour, Ivan Franjo; Mirko Ankes is the other neighbour. All of these homes were damaged on their roofs or elsewhere by these bomblets. The entire casing of the cluster bomb which was emptied during the fall landed on the house of Lojz Kovacic, and the entire casing of the bomb pierced the roof and landed in his kitchen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to give us an estimate of the number of the number of houses that were damaged?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: I know about these cases that I just listed. I know that elsewhere at Pleso there were places where bomblets landed. At least ten homes were damaged, but at the end of the day there was a commission from the Velika Gorica police station which conducted an on-site investigation. In fact, there were five commissions which went around my village to make an accurate record of all the homes that were damaged, and they have the records still.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know if any other people were injured during this operation?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MIKULCIC
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of anyone else in my village having been injured but myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any questions arising from the questions, Ms. Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mikulcic. This brings us to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This brings us to the end of your testimony. Once again, thank you very much for taking your time off to come and testify in this matter. You may now -- you are now excused from further attending court. You may stand down. Thank you very much. And I hope you get --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We hope you get better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess this will be a convenient time? If we can come back at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Our witness will be ready after the break, our next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Court adjourned. Come back at quarter to 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution would call its next witness, Mr. Branko Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May the witness come through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated, sir. Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Lazarevic. Can you hear me okay? Can you understand the translation through your headphones?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I can hear you and I understand the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If at any time you have any difficulty understanding one of my questions, please just say so and I'll try to rephrase it, I'll try to put it more clearly.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I understand. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: My name is Branko Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Where were you born, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Bijeljina, in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: On what date were you born?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I was born on 23 October 1949.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were born in Bosnia. When did you move to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I moved to Croatia in 1970.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just so it's clear, where did you live in May of 1995?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In May 1995 I lived in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now ask you just a few questions about your career in the police. You joined the police force initially in 1971. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you worked as an ordinary policeman until 1977, when you joined the police academy in Zagreb. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: While at the police academy, did you receive any training in on-site investigation procedures?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was a subject called investigations. We worked on that for a few months, maybe even whole semester.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When did you complete your studies at the police academy?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I completed my studies in 1987 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: For a few months I worked at the police station in Crnomerec and Susegrad, and from there I had originally been sent to the academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And where were you first transferred to the municipal SUP or police headquarters in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I was transferred to the municipal SUP of Zagreb on the 1st of September, 1980. 1980, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What positions did you hold during your career at the municipal SUP of Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Initially I worked in the department for prevention of general crime, and there I was an operative in charge of investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And after that did you hold any other positions, besides being an operative in charge of -- perhaps I don't understand. When you say you were an operative in charge of investigations, could you -- could you explain that a little bit.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would say that this was an initial stage. When you first join that department for on-site investigations, you become an inspector for on-site investigations. And for a few years this is what you do. This is the lowest level, and all operatives who become engaged in on-site investigations have to start from that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What positions did you have after that starting level?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: A few years later, having spent some time at that initial level, I became the head of the shift, or shift commander, and I was the shift commander for a few years. I had five or six operatives under me. They worked in my shift. I stayed in that position until 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And what happened in 1990?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Then I was promoted. I became the head of department for on-site investigations. I was in charge of four shifts in the department, and I had between 30 and 40 operatives reporting to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What kind of cases did your department work on?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The on-site investigation department that I was in charge of dealt with the so-called general crimes, which means that we worked on various cases and we performed on-site investigations for everything but traffic accidents. I'm talking about murders, arson, rapes, railway accidents, air traffic accidents, everything that falls under the penal code, save for the road accidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to clear one thing up. You said you became the head of department for on-site investigations. Was there anyone senior to you in the department or were you the -- over all in charge of the department?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In that department I had a chief above me. I was in charge of on-site investigations. There was nobody superior to me in that respect, but I reported to the chief. To make things simple, my department had five sections, and one of the sections was an on-site investigation section and I was the head of that section. And the chief of the department was the person that I reported to. I was subordinated to the chief of department.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. And one other clarification. I think it may have just been a mistake in the transcript. What year did you complete your studies at the police academy?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I was at the academy from 1977 to 1979, and I took my last exam in 1979 and I believe I graduated in 1980, in the month of April of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I'd like to turn your attention to the 2nd of May, 1995. First of all, do you remember what the weather was like on that day, what kind of a day it was?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it -- the day was nice, warm, sunny, no rain or anything, no wind, no precipitation whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And where were you on that morning?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On that morning I was in my office. My working hours were between 7.00 in the morning and 4.00 in the afternoon, and on the 2nd of May, 1995, in the morning, I was in my office. My office was in Zagreb in Djordjiceva Street number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Was there any advanced warning or indication that Zagreb might be attacked that day?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was nothing. As far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Tell us what in fact happened.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I've already told you, on that day I was in my office in Djordjiceva, number 4. At one point in time I heard a noise, it -- an explosion or explosions. I went down to the street and continued towards Zrinjevac. I had heard alarms. I could see fire brigades. People were running, in a state of panic. The distance was not that big. I looked towards the railway station, to the main railway station, towards Strossmayer square and I could see that in the vicinity of the centre police station, in Strossmayer square a few cars were aflame, a few fire brigade vehicles were on their way in order to extinguish the fire. There were a few wounded people. The emergency services are also in Djordjiceva Street at number 26, and it did not take a long time for their ambulances, maybe less than five minutes, to get to the site. And in general terms, there was a state of panic, a state of confusion, as things are when five or six cars are ablaze, when there are wounded on the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately what time it was on the morning of May 2nd that this happened?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This happened before noon. I believe that it was sometime after 10.00 in the morning. After 10.00, maybe 10.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a video. This is trial exhibit 383, and to watch it you'll have to use the Sanction, so if we could please switch to the Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And then the question from me, as always, Your Honour, is, which button do we push?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was going to ask you that question, what is the Sanction in the first place?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sanction is a system that we use to show videos, Your Honour. That's all we use it for. And I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The one marked "video"?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we can broadcast the Sanction here then we'll be able to tell. To broadcast that. [Prosecution counsel confer].

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, you can see it on the regular e-court screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And we'll play the first clip -- I have three short clips that I'd like to show him right now. Could we play the first one, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me just ask a quick question about that first clip. Mr. Lazarevic, are you able to tell us where this video is filmed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The video was filmed in Zagreb, in Strossmayer square, and we have just seen what I described. A few cars were on fire, maybe five or six vehicles that were parked closer to the police station. Maybe some 10 or 15 metres towards Boskoviceva Street. And we also saw the arrival of the fire brigade vehicles and the exercise to extinguish the fire of the cars that were ablaze when the bomb exploded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to show you two more clips that are shorter than that last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: We just paused it and the time code is minute 6:07.2. Mr. Lazarevic, what do we see on our screen right now?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On the screen we can see a bomb, the so-called KB-1, which did not explode. And the photo was taken on the scene of the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, just for the record this clip as well as the following, all three are part of trial exhibit 383.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And the third clip from the same exhibit. [Videotape played].

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Actually, could we start the clip again? My apologies. Start the clip again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, what do we see on the screen right now?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On the screen we can see a dead body. This is Mrs. Ana Mutevelic, who was killed during this incident. The place is the crossroads of Vlaska Street and Draskoviceva Street. The body is covered and marked by number 1 that we see to the left of her head. According to the information that we collected during our investigation, we learned that the lady had sustained injuries while she was riding on a tram. One of the shells had hit the tram that she was in. The lady sustained injuries, and she succumbed to her injuries there and then. She was taken off the tram and she was laid on the pavement as we see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: For the record, the time code is 7 minutes and 41.3 seconds. If we could continue with the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: This is 8 minutes 00.8 seconds on the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, what do we see on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On the screen we can see a dead body. This is Damir Dracic, who also was killed during the shelling, during the rocket attack that is. According to the information that we collected, the gentleman was driving his car at the time a shell fragment or several of them hit the vehicle, pierced the metal, and the glass. The fragments hit the gentleman and injured him. And the gentleman died in the car. The scene is Vlaska Street in front of number 41.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could we continue with the clip, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm done with trial exhibit 383.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, perhaps I've gotten a little ahead of myself, but let me ask you this: After you heard the explosions and you described how you went down and what you saw there, what did you then tell your operatives in the on-site investigation section to do?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: As the head of the on-site investigation section, it was clear to me what had happened and what we had on our hands. I knew that there had to be an on-site investigation. I took immediate measures without wasting a moment I undertook measures in order to gather all the operatives that were available to me, and I deployed them with certain tasks. I sent them out and ordered them to start collecting data. The information started pouring in, and it was with the lapse of time, maybe five, ten, or 15 minutes later, I received information and I realised that not only what I saw had happened when I left my office, I realised that this was not everything that happened, that there were some other locations in town that had been hit by bombs. Having received that information, I realised that I had quite a big task on my hands and that it should be done very fast and very well. That's why I tried to gather as many operatives as possible, especially the most seasoned ones. I did that. I gave them their tasks, and we embarked in an on-site investigation immediately. When the cars that had burnt down were removed, when the dead bodies were removed from the streets - and this is also something that had to be done -- actually it was the first thing that we were supposed to do in order to proceed with our tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Were you able to personally visit any of the other sites, besides the one that you've already described to us?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I went to those sites that were closest to me, that were down-town in the vicinity of my office. As I said, as the information was coming in I realised that the bombs had hit the main building of the police force, that's to say the main administration building near the Croatian cultural association, which is quite close to the street where we saw the cars on fire, perhaps some 50 metres away from the street that we saw. That's the Matica Hrvatska Street. And down that street, which is quite a short one, another street, Petrinska Street, can be found where the police building, the administration building, had been hit, it is at Petrinska 30. I've just mentioned the police premises, but a number of other buildings in the Petrinska Street were hit, as were many cars that were parked on both sides of the street. Quite a number of shops, business premises were damaged, the bombs were landing all the way down to Boskoviceva Street, which covers a distance of perhaps 400 metres from the police administration building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'll ask you -- be asking you some more specific questions about these places during the course of your testimony. Did you go to any of the other sites, for instance Pleso or any of the other places, personally?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I myself took part in conducting on-site investigations in order to relieve the burden on my colleagues. On that day we learnt that the same type of bombs had also landed on the village of Pleso where the Zagreb airport was situated. The village of Pleso is basically a part of the town of Velika Gorica, part of its environs. And I went over there during the day and established that damage was inflicted on the homes there, minor damage was also found at the airport. There was one bomb that landed in front of a shop, commercial premises located at the airport themself -- itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. At this point I'd like to show you a document. The ERN is 03655451 to 5598.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would propose, if it meets Your Honour's approval, to provide hard copies of this report and there's one other report. And the reason is they're quite extensive and he'll be talking about it for a while and we'll have to look at other documents. As Your Honours know, with e-court it's difficult to bounce between documents. I'm certainly aware of Your Honour's preference that we use e-court, as set forth in the guideline but I ask for an exception in these circumstances --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Black, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, here are four copies in English for the court, a copy for the witness, as well as one for the Defence or for the accused if they don't have one. And I would also mention that I have extra copies and I neglected to give them to the interpreters ahead of time, but we'll do that as soon as the usher has a chance so they can follow along. Thanks very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, do you recognise this document that's been handed to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is a photocopy of the record of an on-site investigation I myself drafted after the on-site investigation was completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In fact, does it bear your signature on the last page?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, how -- how did you go about compiling this -- this report?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Martic doesn't have the report before him. Could the -- my learned friend spare a copy for him?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, you were just about to explain how you compiled the information which you've included -- which you included in this report. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've touched upon the issue already. I myself went to the scene of the incident. Since the site where the bombs landed, including the sites where buildings and vehicles were damaged as well as the sites where there were injured people, were quite numerous, I had to give specific assignments to my operatives and send them to various streets. They immediately proceeded to conduct their on-site investigations, and as I said I myself conducted some, too. Each of my colleagues who conducted on-site investigations on given locations produced their respective reports with their findings and photographic material. Therefore, as a result we had written material covering each and one of these on-site investigations that I took possession of and compiled a general report that covered all the individual reports. And I signed it. Therefore, it is the product of my work and of the work of my colleagues from the on-site investigations section. Their reports, which were the basis for my main record of on-site investigations, are attached to my report and can be found in the operative files of my section.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And just so it's clear, the underlying reports by your colleagues, those aren't attached to the document that you have in front of you now, but they're attached back in -- in the files back in Zagreb. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, precisely. Had I conducted the on-site investigation on my own, single-handedly, it would have taken me ten to 15 days to complete the investigations, perhaps even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In fact, how long did it take you to compile the document which you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It's hard for me to reconstruct how long it took me to write the document we have before us here, but I do know that I was working on the case the entire days on the 2nd and 3rd of May, 1995. I processed the information, attached the medical documentation to it, and then I wrote the report. The entire process took 40 days. Let me clarify. The component part of the report consists of photographic documentation, sketches, diagrams, observations by forensic examiners, and it took me as many days to compile all these elements which form the component part of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think it's clear, thank you. In fact, I'd like to go -- this report contains a lot of detail. I'd like to go through it fairly quickly. And consequently, I'm just going to ask you a number of questions but not questions about every detailed aspect about the report. My first question is: What locations are discussed in this document that you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The document before us covers the following locations: Strossmayer's square; Matica Hrvatska Street, Petrinska Street; Boskoviceva Street; Draskoviceva Street; Vlaska Street; the high school at Krizeviceva [phoen] Street; and the location in the Velika Gorica area, that's to say Pleso.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. And how would you describe all those locations that you've just mentioned? Are they -- are they central? Are they isolated? Are they ordinarily crowded, not crowded? Can you just give us a feel for those locations, please?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Almost all these locations, including Pleso, were locations which were full of people at the time of these incidents. There were many pedestrians and cars on the move, including public transportation, that's to say trams. At the time in town of some 1 million inhabitants and given the time of the day, there were quite a few people on the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: As far as you know, are there any military buildings or facilities at these various locations you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there isn't a single military feature in the immediate vicinity of the locations I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I've asked you now about the locations discussed in the document. What kinds of damage -- different kinds of damage or what kind of things were damaged, as discussed in your report?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The report discusses the damage inflicted on numerous cars, buildings, even on the roof-tops of these buildings, shops. There were pock-marks on paved areas, typical of those normally inflicted by bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that's a sufficient overview. Let me ask you about some specific parts of the report. If you could turn to page 50 in the original, the B/C/S version. It's page 46 in English. Page 50 in the document that -- in the hard copy in front of you, sir.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I think I've located it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you'll see that it's also on the computer screen in front of you if you just want to double-check. The ERN number there is 03655451. What is discussed at this page of your report, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could scroll down a bit more. That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 50 of this on-site report, there is the description of the body of Ana Mutevelic, who was injured while riding on a tram, as I said a moment ago. She was then taken off the tram and laid down on the sidewalk. She had visible injuries on her body, all over her body. In medical terms, she had a number of explosive wounds, and the largest of them was on her head near her ear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you to look at the next page, page 51.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It's the same page in the English, Your Honours, just a little further down on page 46.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What is discussed here, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On this page there's the description of the dead body of Damir Dracic, who was lying next to his car, on the pavement. There was a multitude of explosive wounds all over his body which resulted in his death, which led to his death.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could please turn to the next page, 52, in the original, it's page 47 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What's discussed at the top of page 52, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On this page we can see the description of the dead body of Stjepan Krhen. He died in the courtyard at Vlaska number 41. In front of the company doorman's booth. He also had sustained several injuries on his body, on his chest, and on his legs. And he also succumbed to these wounds immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you look at the bottom of that same page and tell me what's mentioned there, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This is the description of Mrs. Ivanka Kovac at the moment of shelling or rocket attack, she sustained wounds. When the ambulance arrived, she still showed some signs of life and that's why she was transported to the trauma clinic in Draskoviceva Street. This hospital is some 700 metres away from the place where she was wound; in other words, it didn't take long for her to be transported to the hospital. Still, she succumbed to her wounds maybe ten minutes after the arrival at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll return to Mrs. Kovac a little bit later. Let me ask you now to look at page 70 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It's page 63 in English, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, what is discussed beginning at this page and on the following pages, just generally?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Here I described the persons who had been wounded. First there is their names as well as the indication of the hospital to which those people were transported after having been found. Furthermore, this page contains information on the location of their wounds; in other words, where the wounds were on their body. And also this page contains the medical qualification of every person's wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just noticed that this document does contain some addresses, so I would ask that perhaps the public video feed that goes out could not show the document. And then what I'll do is arrange to have a redacted copy put into evidence at a later date. I'm sorry that I didn't do that in advance. I don't think we need to have any orders, I just think that the video booth can assist me in not publicly broadcast that part; they can just use the video of the witness instead of showing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I notice that there are some pages that are blocked out. Are those not the --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You're exactly right, Your Honour. I had thought that we had redacted all the necessary information, but I think I'm seeing that maybe there's some more that should be redacted. Just -- I don't think it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Very well then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just as a courtesy to those people then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Very well then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, the report distinguishes between serious bodily injury and minor bodily injury. Could you just explain the difference for us, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'll try and explain the difference for you, although I'm an expert in crime prevention I'm not a physician. A doctor would be better suited to provide you with that explanation; however, based on my long practice and experience in on-site investigations where I have encountered a number of such cases, I can tell you that in our legislation there is a -- a distinction between a minor injury and a serious injury. To put it simply, minor injuries are those injuries which cause a minor impairment. We're talking about haematomas, minor injuries that do not hurt any vital organs, when there are no fractures. In any case, when the person is slightly wounded and when the consequences are not great. Heavy or serious injuries would be brain injuries, almost all and every fracture, save for the nose fracture without any shifts. We're talking about the fracture of all bones, save for the bone in the nose. Also we're talking about organ injuries, injuries to the blood vessels, and I believe that I have covered everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. And who made the determination of whether an injury was serious or minor that we see in your report?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Every person that is mentioned in the record on on-site investigation was examined by a doctor and the qualification of their injury was provided by a doctor. I waited for all the medical reports to arrive at the police station. I'm talking about the medical reports on every of those injured persons that were examined. Every doctor that sees a wounded person is duty-bound to compile a report on the exam that contains the basic data on the identity of the wounded person, the time and place of injury, the way injuries were sustained; furthermore, the description of the injury or injuries; furthermore, the diagnosis, and the diagnosis has to be provided in the Latin language and also in Croatian. And finally, every doctor is duty-bound to specify the medical qualification of the injury, and the medical qualification is what I just tried to explain to you. I tried to explain the distinction between a minor injury and a serious injury. I looked at all of those medical reports and I included into my record all those reports. I actually copied all those medical reports. I included a location of the wound and the medical qualification of every wound. Furthermore, every medical report was enclosed with my on-site investigation report, so you can see for yourself that my record is a true copy of the reports that I had been provided with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I'll ask you to look again at a specific part of the report. If you could look at number 75 on this list of injured. You'll find it on page 81?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's page 71 of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, who is named here at number 75 on this list?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Under 75 you can see the name of Ivan Brodar. He was born in 1918. During this incident he suffered multiple trauma of the head, chest, and lower extremities. He was transported to the trauma clinic, but he succumbed to his wounds on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And so does --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No, please continue.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: During the rocket attack I believe that he was 77 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. And what's captured here in this report reflects his condition on -- as of the 2nd of May, 1995. Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the moment when the record was compiled and the date it bears is the date when the incident happened, he was still alive. He succumbed to his wounds later on. There are medical documents to prove that. There's also a pathology report. He died. He succumbed to his wounds and there are autopsy reports to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll return to Ivan Brodar in just a moment. Those are all my questions -- my specific questions, however, about this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that it be admitted into evidence and that it receive an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The report is admitted into evidence. And may it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 799, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I'd like to show the witness another document. This is 65 ter number 2251, if we could see that on the e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What do we see on the screen in front of us, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On the screen we can see autopsy report. This is for Mrs. Ivanka Kovac, and this was performed at the Institute for Forensic Medicine and Crime, Salata number 11. This is a description of the wounds that the doctor could establish. There's also the diagnosis of those wounds. And finally at the end of the document is the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And what cause of death does it mention?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I can see only the first page. I don't see anything further. In any case, the cause of death, as far as I can remember, were multiple injuries to the head, chest, and extremities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Is it possible to turn to the next page, please? And I think if we scroll down to the bottom of that page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we have it. It says: "Explosive wounds of the head, of the body, and the extremities." This is the cause of death. The doctor signed this, Dr. Stjepan Gusic is the forensic expert, and on the left-hand side you see the signature of Professor Dusan Zecevic, who is the head of the institute for forensic medicine, and they are both forensic experts in pathology.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document be admitted into evidence and be given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence and may it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be 800.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: One more document for today. If we could see document 2258 on the screen, please. And if we could turn to the next page in fact, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, what is this document that we're looking at now?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Here we have another autopsy report by doctor's of the school of medicine. His name is Professor Skavic, and it was compiled after the autopsy of Mr. Ivan Brodar, who had been injured in Draskoviceva Street, and he died on the following day at the trauma clinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was it the following day or the 3rd of June?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, did you hear His Honour's question?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe I did, and I reply that Mr. Brodar died one day later after having been brought to the hospital. He died on the 3rd of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: We just have a little confusion. He was injured on the 2nd of May, 1995. So would -- do you see that confusion?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes. Can you confirm, based on this document, when -- what date he in fact died?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It says here that he died on the 3rd of June. I can't be a hundred per cent sure, but I think he died on the 3rd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In any event, he did -- did he ever recover from the injuries he suffered on the 2nd of May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, no. No, the gentleman died, and the cause of death were the injuries that he suffered as a result of the bomb explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could perhaps turn to the next page in the document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you scroll down a little? I don't see the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes. And what does it say is the cause of his death?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The cause of death are injuries. These are all in Latin. I believe that there should be the diagnosis in Croatian as well. There should be a diagnosis in Croatian. Maybe this is not the right place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Perhaps if we continue to the next page, and I apologise for not having identified this page in advance. Does that clarify things, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This is an autopsy report. This is a medical description, but I believe, as a matter of fact, that there's no doubt --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If we just scroll down to the bottom of the page, please, the last sentence there. Yeah, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: "The pneumonia that developed during the course of treatment after the patient sustained explosive injuries is the cause of violent death which is closely connected and is directly connected with the wounds," and this is the finding by the two professors of forensic medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this be admitted, and then we can end for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence, may it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 801, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: My apologies for going a few minutes over. I'm happy to take the adjournment for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Court will adjourn now. We'll start tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 15th day of June, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.
